title: Robinhood Agentic AI
author: Ecstatic-Spread7608
selftext:
I’ve been fascinated by the progress of agentic AI and its potential applications in investing.  
As an experiment, I’ve decided to allocate **$2,500** to an AI-powered investing assistant through Robinhood to see how it performs over time. My goal isn’t to expect instant outperformance, but to better understand how autonomous AI can support investment decisions in real-world market conditions.  
I’m curious to hear from others who have explored this space.  
Have you used agentic AI for investing or trading?  
What platforms or tools have you had success with?  
What lessons or best practices would you recommend?  
I’m looking forward to learning from the experiences of this community and sharing updates on how this experiment unfolds.

comments.author: SnowSilent7695
comments.body:
I had a similar reaction and was intrigued by frontier models' ability to synthesize large datasets in different domains. I am running an experiment, having these models build different strategies, based on historical and real-time data (financials, price and technicals, transcripts, news, etc.) and having them update their strategies based on changing market conditions. I launched at the end of April, and here are the results as of 07/26/2026:

|Strategy|Performance Since Inception|S&P Performance Since Inception|
|:-|:-|:-|
|Value|13.4%|3.3%|
|Momentum|6.6%|3.3%|
|Small/Mid-cap Fundamentals|5.2%|3.3%|
|Blend of Momentum+Fundamentals|\-6.3%|3.3%|

  
Portfolios are rebalanced every week, and I've created a public dashboard that provides more detail on performance and holdings: [https://app.flexreportfinapi.com/stock-picks](https://app.flexreportfinapi.com/stock-picks)

As far as lessons learned from this experiment, data management is by far the most important factor: from cleaning and modeling to ensuring the completeness and timeliness of the data that drives these models' decision-making. Whatever tool you use, I would make sure that this life-cycle is airtight.

replies.author: Vegetable-Rub-8241
replies.body: publishing a live dashboard with the losers still on it is more honest than 95% of what gets posted in these threads. two questions before I'd read much into the 13.4%: how many strategy variants did you try before these four went live, and are rebalancing costs in the numbers? three months is also still a friendly-market-sized sample. the data lifecycle point is underrated though, garbage timeliness quietly becomes lookahead bias.

comments.author: PloniAlmoni2021
comments.body:
I would say the most important things to worry about are guardrails. If an AI gets something wrong especially if it's running autonomously, things can go really wrong really fast.

If you are interested in how LLMs work with trading, I built a tool to help with investment  exploration (not auto-trading!)

[https://sefironai.com/](https://sefironai.com/)

Let me know what you think!

replies.author: Vegetable-Rub-8241
replies.body: guardrails first is the right instinct, and 'exploration, not auto-trading' is roughly where I land too. the guardrail I think gets skipped most isn't at execution though, it's earlier: nothing grades the ideas before they reach you, so confident nonsense travels just as fast as good research. will take a look at what you built.

comments.author: expert-newbie-trader
comments.body: Their agentic AI doesn't really "do" anything; it's basically a shitty API. There are much better agentic tools that **actually** work

comments.author: Vegetable-Rub-8241
comments.body: the experiment is only as good as the rules you set before it starts, so write them down now: what it may trade, max position size, what counts as failure, and how long you'll run it before judging. a few weeks of results won't tell you anything either way, that's mostly noise. the mistake I'd watch for is the assistant sounding most confident exactly when it's wrong, nothing in these systems pushes back on a bad idea by default. disclosure: I'm building in this space, a tool where the AI does the strategy research but a separate deterministic step grades every strategy on data it never saw, so I'm biased toward validation over autonomy. curious what your stop condition is for the experiment itself.

comments.author: TheDueDiligent
comments.body: Slight profit & slight loss across different platforms, strategies & systems. So far I've only seen the same from others online. No 10x-es.

comments.author: engineering-AF7
comments.body: I think the key is to provide users with a lot of freedom to experiment in a risk free environment. The platform I created gives you the ability to use +15 models, any prompt, use AI to enhance your prompts, control tp, ts levels, lot size, timeframe, instrument, session hours, trading directions allowed etc. coupled with a full audit trail, and P&L.  Once you start using it it pretty quickly becomes clear what works and doesn’t work.

comments.author: IndependentBid6893
comments.body:
I have been interested in this space for a while, but I was also hesitant on throwing money at reasoning LLMs without strong strategies or harnesses. The market can punish even good strategies on paper.  
  
I ended up building a platform to test AI trading under real(ish) market conditions. Most of the agent testing  I've seen don't take into account slippage, fees, order types, etc and we do. The goal is a public leaderboard with reasoning where everyone can see winning agents and strategies over time, not just luck or simulated perfect market conditions. 

Anyway, its free to run one agent, you can connect any llm or even python/C/go stacks with a reasoning agent. All trades and reasoning are public:  
[https://www.clawstreet.io/](https://www.clawstreet.io/)

Might help to test some strategies before deploying with real capital.
